questions.question_text: To create an instance of a programmer-defined type, what is the correct order for these steps?
options: Assign values to attributes, define a class, instantiate an object.
Instantiate an object, define a class, assign values to attributes.
Define a class, assign values to attributes, instantiate an object.
Define a class, instantiate an object, assign values to attributes.
rationales: You can't assign attributes before you instantiate an object.
You can't instantiate an object before you define its class.
You can't assign attributes before you instantiate an object.
You have to define a class, instantiate an object, and assign values to attributes, in that order.

questions.question_text:
These statements are intended to define a `Date` class and create a `Date` object. What is wrong with them?

```
def Date:
    """Represents a day of the year."""

date = Date()
date.year = 2024
date.month = 'January'
date.day = 11
```
options: You can't have a class named `Date` and a variable named `date`.
All of the attributes have to have the same type.
The syntax is not correct for adding attributes to the object.
A class definition has to start with `class`, not `def`.
rationales: It is legal -- and common -- for a class name and a variable to be the same word, but the class name starts with an uppercase letter.
The attributes of an object can be any type, and they don't have to be the same.
Dot notation is used to set the value of an attribute and to read the value.
A class definition has to start with `class`. A function definition starts with `def`.

questions.question_text:
Which of these is a correct description of this function? You can assume that `date` is a `Date` object that has a `day` attribute.

```
def increment_day(date):
    date.day += 1
    return date
```
options: It is a pure function that returns `None`.
It is an impure function that returns `None`.
It is a pure function that returns a `Date` object.
It is an impure function that returns a `Date` object.
rationales: This function modifies an attribute of the `Date` object it gets as a parameter, so it is an impure function. And it returns a reference to the same object, not `None`.
This function returns a reference to a `Date` object, not `None`.
This function modifies an attribute of the `Date` object it gets as a parameter, so it is an impure function.
This function modifies an attribute of the `Date` object it gets as a parameter, so it is an impure function -- and it returns a reference to the same `Date` object.

questions.question_text:
Suppose `today` refers to a `Date` object, and we run this code:

```
def set_date(date, val):
    date.date = val

set_date(today, 27)
```

Which of these is true afterward?
options: It caused an error, because `date` is already the name of a parameter.
The parameter `date` was changed to `27`, but `today` is unchanged.
The `Date` object that `today` refers to has an attribute called `date` whose value is `27`.
rationales: A parameter and an attribute can have the same name without conflict: the parameter is a variable in the function's frame and the attribute belongs to the object.
The function never assigns a new value to `today` or to `date`; it assigns to an attribute of the object they both refer to.
`date.date = val` does not change the parameter `date` -- it still refers to the `Date` object -- and because `date` and `today` refer to the same object, the change is visible through `today`.

Inside the function, `date` refers to the same object as `today`, so `date.date = val` creates an attribute of that object. Functions like `make_time` in this chapter use the same names for parameters and attributes on purpose.
